title: Recovery anchor resume must not re-enter runInstall
description: Objective: make a resume after a crash in the anchor install window idempotent instead of re-running the install. Register item 2 of 11 from task-963cf1d125134c6193b7af0e53deeac3 (2026-08-14 product audit; verified real, classified low). RE-MEASURED STILL OPEN at HEAD 192360e: packages/store/src/recovery-anchor-install.ts:224 `runInstall`, with fault points `fault?.("SWITCH")` at :255 and `fault?.("INSTALLED_MARKER")` at :259. A crash between the SWITCH publish and the INSTALLED marker leaves the anchor having SELECTED a database with no marker recorded, and resume re-enters runInstall rather than recognising the completed switch. recovery-anchor-contracts.ts:36 defines RECOVERY_ANCHOR_STATES as PREPARED|INSTALLED and :253 documents that INSTALLED means the anchor SELECTED a database, not that recovery finished - so the state needed to recognise the window exists. Deliverable: resume detects that the switch already landed and completes the install by recording the marker, rather than re-running the switch. NOT in scope: the backup generation publish ordering (register item 1 owns that), restore controller policy, or the two-slot binding mechanics. Verification: pnpm --filter @moe/store typecheck && pnpm --filter @moe/store test.
definitionOfDone: A resume after a crash between the SWITCH publish and the INSTALLED marker completes the install by recording the marker, and does NOT re-execute the switch - proven by driving the existing SWITCH/INSTALLED_MARKER fault points, not by a test-local reimplementation.
Re-running the install on an already-INSTALLED anchor is idempotent and returns the existing exact outcome, never a second switch or a duplicate marker.

A resume that cannot prove the switch landed refuses with the exact stable store reason code and layer rather than guessing in either direction - an ambiguous window stays UNKNOWN and does not install.
Generated resume cases assert a nonzero exact cardinality covering each fault point, and mutating the already-switched detection turns a named test red.
Fresh pnpm --filter @moe/store typecheck && pnpm --filter @moe/store test exits 0.
taskRails: Detection must rest on durable evidence that the switch landed, never on a wall-clock, a retry counter, or the absence of an error.
Do not weaken the single-shot guarantee: recognising a completed switch must not make a genuine second switch possible.
Every refusal test pins the exact stable reason code and the refusing layer, not merely that resume failed.
Target <=250 physical lines per production source; split before 400.

implementationPlan.description: TDD RED FIRST. In packages/store/src/recovery-anchor.test.ts, drive installRecoveryAnchor to the SWITCH point using the existing injectFault seam - fault?.("INSTALLED_MARKER") in recovery-anchor-install.ts is the point to abort at, since it fires AFTER the switch has been published and BEFORE the marker is written. Then call installRecoveryAnchor again with the same request and assert two things: the result is INSTALLED, and the protocol was NOT re-entered - assert that writeInactiveSlot and the stampIncarnation transaction did not run on the second call, by observing the seam rather than by inspecting bytes, since re-running them is the actual harm. This is RED today: settledInstall (recovery-anchor.ts:108-115) returns null unless `stored.state === "INSTALLED"`, so the post-switch/pre-marker record falls through to prepareRecoveryAnchor + runInstall and re-enters the protocol. Record that red before touching production.
implementationPlan.note:
TDD RED recorded, and it fails naming the exact boundary that must not re-run.

  AssertionError: boundary INACTIVE_INSTALL must not be crossed again:
  expected [ 'PREPARE', 'INACTIVE_INSTALL', ...(6) ] to not include 'INACTIVE_INSTALL'

Eight fault points observed on the SECOND call — the full protocol, re-entered from PREPARE. That is the defect itself, not a fixture problem.

I VERIFIED THE PLAN'S LOAD-BEARING CLAIM BEFORE WRITING ANYTHING. The whole fix rests on `state === "PREPARED" && currentSlot === targetSlot` being unreachable before the switch; if any other path could produce that pair, the new arm would skip a real install and report INSTALLED over an unwritten slot — worse than the bug being fixed. Traced every writer:
- recovery-install-contracts.ts:11 RECOVERY_BINDING_SLOTS is exactly ["ACTIVE","PENDING"], and selectInactiveSlot (recovery-anchor.ts:50-52) returns the opposite member, so it can never return its argument.
- The prepare path builds the record as buildAnchorRecord(request, { current, target: selectInactiveSlot(current) }, "PREPARED") — target is BY CONSTRUCTION the other slot, so current !== target at PREPARE.
- resealAnchorRecord has exactly TWO production call sites, both in runInstall: :256 sets currentSlot = targetSlot with state still PREPARED (the switch), and :260 sets state = INSTALLED.
- The other currentSlot mentions are reads, not writes: recovery-anchor.ts:161 and :184 read stored.currentSlot in discardRecoveryAnchor/inspectRecoveryAnchor, and :191 returns it in the inspect result. discardRecoveryAnchor never writes the anchor record.
So the pair is produced at exactly one place and cleared at exactly one place. The signature is unambiguous. Claim holds.

THE TEST OBSERVES THE SEAM, NOT THE BYTES — this is the difference between a real test and one that passes either way. The harm is that writeInactiveSlot and stampIncarnation RUN against what is now the LIVE slot; a re-entry that happens to succeed still leaves a correct-looking anchor on disk, so asserting disk content would pass while the protocol was re-entered. The test records which fault boundaries the second call crosses and requires the six protocol boundaries to be absent.

I ASSERT THE SIX BOUNDARIES INDIVIDUALLY AND THEN THE EMPTY LIST. `expect(observed).toEqual([])` alone would be strictly stronger but, when it fails, says only "expected 8 items to equal []" — it never names which boundary re-ran. The per-boundary loop carries the message "boundary INACTIVE_INSTALL must not be crossed again", which is what made this red immediately legible.

THE WINDOW IS ASSERTED, NOT ASSUMED. Before resuming, the test inspects the stored record and pins state === "PREPARED" with currentSlot === targetSlot. Without that, a fixture that failed to reach the window (crashing earlier, or the fault never firing) would make the resume trivially correct and the test vacuous.

ONE FIXTURE HAZARD CHECKED RATHER THAN DISCOVERED LATER: request() mints a fresh temp anchorRoot and fresh sqlite bytes on every call, so I confirmed computePreparedIdentity (recovery-anchor-record.ts:124-137) covers only codec version, generationDigest, incarnationRef, keyEpochRef, preparedAt and restoreCommandId — NOT the payload. So the second call carries the same prepared identity despite different database bytes, and the resume is a genuine same-command resume rather than a new command.

Sizes at HEAD e6597e4 (HEAD moved from the 192360e the plan measured; re-checked): recovery-anchor.ts 198, recovery-anchor-install.ts 263 (already 13 over target), recovery-anchor-contracts.ts 260, recovery-anchor.test.ts now 790. Production untouched this step.

implementationPlan.description: Extend the completion guard to cover the post-switch window. recovery-anchor.ts:108-115 `settledInstall` currently recognises only a fully completed install: it reads the stored anchor, returns null unless `state === "INSTALLED"`, and otherwise matches on preparedIdentity. Add recognition of the OTHER settled state - `state === "PREPARED"` together with `currentSlot === targetSlot` - which is reachable ONLY after the switch has been published, because before the switch currentSlot names the other slot. Keep the preparedIdentity check on both arms: an anchor belonging to a different command must still refuse rather than be adopted. This needs no new durable field; the record already carries currentSlot (contracts :107), targetSlot (:121) and state (:120), and runInstall's own post-switch record is exactly `resealAnchorRecord(prepared, { currentSlot: prepared.targetSlot })` with state still PREPARED.
implementationPlan.note:
Recognition arm landed and the step-1 red is green: 43 passed (43), exit 0. Steps 2 and 3 were coupled by a file-size constraint, so the marker-only completion landed with the recognition rather than after it; step 3's note will cover its own checks.

THE GUARD NOW READS:
  if (stored === null || "ok" in stored) return null;
  if (stored.preparedIdentity !== computePreparedIdentity(request)) return null;
  if (stored.state === "INSTALLED") { return ...outcome: "INSTALLED"... }
  if (stored.currentSlot !== stored.targetSlot) return null;
  return markInstalled(anchorPath(request.anchorRoot), stored);

I MOVED THE IDENTITY CHECK ABOVE THE STATE CHECK ON PURPOSE. Previously it sat last, reachable only after `state === "INSTALLED"` had already passed. Adding a second settled arm underneath it would have left that arm unguarded, which is exactly the risk the plan named — a different command's anchor being adopted because "the switch already landed". Hoisting it makes one identity gate cover both arms. This is not a behaviour change for the existing path: a non-INSTALLED record with a mismatched identity returned null before at the state check and returns null now at the identity check.

WHERE THE MARKER WRITE WENT, AND WHY NOT WHERE THE PLAN SUGGESTED. The plan preferred putting it beside runInstall in recovery-anchor-install.ts, but step 5 also forbids growing that file — it was already 263 lines against a 250 target. I measured the suggested shape: removing runInstall's 3 tail lines and adding a ~14-line exported helper nets 263 -> 274. That grows it. So I took the plan's own stated fallback and split: new module packages/store/src/recovery-anchor-marker.ts (36 lines) holding markInstalled, imported by both writers.

RESULT — NEITHER EXISTING FILE GREW PAST TARGET:
  recovery-anchor-install.ts 263 -> 262 (it SHRANK; 3 tail lines became 1 call plus 1 import)
  recovery-anchor.ts 198 -> 210
  recovery-anchor-marker.ts 36 (new)
Both writers of the INSTALLED marker now share one implementation, which was the plan's actual goal — two encoders of the same durable record would be free to drift.

I RULED OUT AN IMPORT CYCLE RATHER THAN ASSUMING ONE. recovery-anchor.ts already imports from recovery-anchor-install.js (anchorPath, readStoredAnchor, runInstall, slotDirectory, verifySlot), so putting the helper in recovery-anchor.ts and importing it back into install would have closed a cycle. The marker module instead depends only on contracts, fs and record — grep confirms none of those three import recovery-anchor-install. It also takes the anchor FILE PATH, not the root, specifically because anchorPath is defined in recovery-anchor-install.ts; resolving the root inside the marker module would have re-closed the cycle. That reason is written into the module's doc comment so nobody "tidies" the signature later.

.js BRIDGE ADDED. packages/store uses the bridge convention throughout (recovery-anchor-fs.js is `export * from "./recovery-anchor-fs.ts";`), so recovery-anchor-marker.js carries the matching one line. This is invisible to both vitest and tsc — only a child-process probe would catch its absence — so it was added with the module rather than left to a later gate.

VERIFIED BEFORE CODING, since the whole arm rests on it: `currentSlot === targetSlot` cannot occur before the switch. RECOVERY_BINDING_SLOTS is exactly ["ACTIVE","PENDING"]; selectInactiveSlot returns the opposite member and so can never return its argument; the prepare path builds every record with target = selectInactiveSlot(current); and resealAnchorRecord has exactly two production call sites, both in runInstall (:256 the switch, :260 the marker). One producer, one consumer.

implementationPlan.description: Complete the install by writing the MARKER ONLY, never by re-running. For the post-switch state recognised in step 2, finish exactly as runInstall's final two lines do - `resealAnchorRecord(switched, { state: "INSTALLED" })` published through publishFileAtomically to anchorPath - and return the same {anchor, ok, outcome: "INSTALLED"} shape. Do NOT call writeInactiveSlot, stampIncarnation, persistFileDurably, persistSlotDurably or verifySlot on this path: after the switch, `currentSlot === targetSlot`, so those writes would land in the slot that readers are NOW resolving. That is not a theoretical concern - recovery-anchor.ts's own doc comment above settledInstall already states it: 're-entering the protocol would write the restored payload into the slot that is now LIVE - the one thing this module exists to never do.' The guard was simply one condition short of covering the window its comment describes. Prefer putting the marker-only completion beside runInstall in recovery-anchor-install.ts so both writers of the marker share one implementation.
implementationPlan.note:
Marker-only completion is in place and proven not to re-enter. recovery-anchor.test.ts 43 passed (43). See step 2's note for why the helper became its own module rather than growing recovery-anchor-install.ts.

THE COMPLETION PATH IS markInstalled(anchorFilePath, switched), and it is the ONLY writer of the marker:
  const installed = resealAnchorRecord(switched, { state: "INSTALLED" });
  await publishFileAtomically(anchorFilePath, encodeAnchorRecord(installed));
  return Object.freeze({ anchor: installed, ok: true as const, outcome: "INSTALLED" as const });
runInstall's tail is now `return markInstalled(anchorPath(request.anchorRoot), switched);`, so the resume and the install do not merely produce the same SHAPE — they execute the same bytes. Shape equality was the step's requirement; identity of implementation is strictly stronger and removes the drift the plan was worried about.

THE FORBIDDEN CALLS ARE ABSENT, checked with a positive control rather than by reading. grep -E "writeInactiveSlot|stampIncarnation|persistFileDurably|persistSlotDurably|verifySlot" over recovery-anchor-marker.ts returns 0. The identical pattern over recovery-anchor-install.ts returns 14, so the pattern does match these names and the zero is a measurement. The behavioural proof is stronger than either: step 1's test asserts the resume crossed ZERO fault boundaries (`expect(observed).toEqual([])`), and those five writers all sit behind fault points.

implementationPlan.description: Keep the ambiguous cases refusing, and prove idempotence. Assert that a stored anchor whose preparedIdentity does NOT match the request still refuses on BOTH arms with the existing exact stable code and layer - the new arm must not become a way to adopt another command's anchor. Assert that a PREPARED record whose currentSlot does NOT equal targetSlot (the genuine pre-switch state) still proceeds to a normal install rather than being mistaken for a completed switch, since that is the case the new condition must not swallow. Assert that calling installRecoveryAnchor a third time is idempotent and returns the same record without writing again. Cover each fault point with generated cases asserting an exact non-zero cardinality, so a fault point added later without a case fails the count instead of being skipped silently.
implementationPlan.note:
All four requirements landed and DRILLED. recovery-anchor.test.ts + recovery-anchor-refusals.test.ts: 73 passed (73), exit 0.

THREE MUTATION DRILLS, EACH REDDENING A DIFFERENT NAMED TEST. DoD 4 asks that mutating the already-switched detection turn a named test red; I drilled the arm in all three directions it can be wrong rather than only the one the DoD names.

DRILL A — arm TOO BROAD (delete `if (stored.currentSlot !== stored.targetSlot) return null;`): 7 tests RED, led by "still runs a full install when the crash landed BEFORE the switch", plus every per-boundary resume case from INACTIVE_INSTALL through SWITCH. This is the dangerous direction — the arm swallowing a genuine pre-switch PREPARED record and reporting INSTALLED over a slot that was never written. Seven independent tests stand in front of it.

DRILL B — arm NEVER FIRES (restore the original `if (stored.state !== "INSTALLED") return null;`): 1 test RED, "records the marker without crossing a single install boundary again". That is the original defect, reproduced exactly, and the step-1 test is what catches it.

DRILL C — identity guard scoped back to the INSTALLED arm only: 1 test RED, "refuses a different command's fence over the post-switch window, by exact code and layer", failing with `expected true to be false` — the intruder's install SUCCEEDED. This proves the identity hoist I made in step 2 is load-bearing rather than cosmetic: without it, a different restore command adopts the crashed command's post-switch anchor and is handed a completed install.

Restored from a pristine copy after each drill; sha256 of recovery-anchor.ts back to 0d98641c4cdec18e76f3eaef6a7ccb2e46b9df80efd718e78da03b766b9fae99 and `git status --porcelain` on it clean-relative-to-my-own-edit. I kept the pristine copy OUTSIDE the repo and restored by file copy, never `git checkout`, which would have reverted the file to HEAD and destroyed the whole fix.

THE FOUR REQUIREMENTS:
1. FOREIGN IDENTITY REFUSES, BY EXACT CODE AND LAYER, ON BOTH ENTRY POINTS — and they are DIFFERENT codes, which is the point. installRecoveryAnchor gives RECOVERY_ANCHOR_INCARNATION_REUSED; resumeRecoveryAnchor screens one layer earlier and gives RECOVERY_ANCHOR_COMMAND_MISMATCH. Both pinned with layer RECOVERY_ANCHOR. Asserting merely "refused" would let either layer answer and never notice which one did — and drill C shows the assertion is live. The test also checks the window survives the refusal untouched: still PREPARED, still owned by RESTORE_COMMAND_ID.
2. THE PRE-SWITCH CASE STILL INSTALLS. Crash at SWITCH (before the publish), then assert the stored record is PREPARED with currentSlot !== targetSlot — the genuine pre-switch state — and that the resume crosses ALL eight boundaries, `expect(observed).toEqual([...RECOVERY_ANCHOR_FAULT_POINTS])`. Asserting the full ordered list rather than "it installed" is what makes drill A redden here.
3. THIRD CALL IS IDEMPOTENT AND WRITES NOTHING. Same anchor returned, zero fault boundaries crossed, and — the part that actually distinguishes it — the anchor file's mtimeMs is unchanged. Byte-identical content would look the same whether or not it was republished, since the record encodes deterministically; only the untouched file proves no second write.
4. GENERATED CASES WITH A HAND-WRITTEN CARDINALITY. One resume case per declared boundary, `expect(resumeCases.length).toBe(8)` and `expect(RECOVERY_ANCHOR_FAULT_POINTS.length).toBe(8)` written as literals rather than derived from the array under test. A sweep that silently generated zero cases would otherwise pass, and a ninth boundary added later now fails the count instead of being skipped in silence. Each case asserts the resume reaches INSTALLED with currentSlot === targetSlot — never half-selecting, never selecting the other slot.

planningNotes.approachesConsidered:
WHERE TO PUT THE RECOGNITION. Adding a third RECOVERY_ANCHOR_STATE (e.g. SWITCHED) written between the two publishes was considered and REJECTED: it adds a durable write inside the very window being closed, enlarging the window rather than removing it, and it changes a frozen state vocabulary that anchorDigest covers. CHOSEN: derive the state from fields already on the record. The signature is exact, needs no extra write, and cannot itself be interrupted.

WHERE TO PUT THE COMPLETION. Extending settledInstall in recovery-anchor.ts keeps the recognition next to its existing sibling, but the marker WRITE belongs beside runInstall's own final two lines so both writers share one implementation - otherwise the marker is published from two places that can drift. That is why step 3 splits recognition (recovery-anchor.ts) from completion (recovery-anchor-install.ts). recovery-anchor-install.ts is already 13 lines over the 250 target, so if the helper cannot fit, splitting that file is the correct move rather than growing it toward 400.

WHY NOT JUST RE-RUN IDEMPOTENTLY. Making runInstall safe to re-run from the top was considered and rejected outright: it would require writeInactiveSlot and stampIncarnation to be safe against the LIVE slot, which is the exact invariant the module is built to protect. Recognising the settled state is strictly safer than making the dangerous path survivable.
planningNotes.risks:
THE WHOLE FIX RESTS ON ONE CLAIM - that `state === "PREPARED" && currentSlot === targetSlot` is unreachable before the switch. I verified it from runInstall's own sequence, but adversarial review must trace EVERY writer of currentSlot to confirm no other path produces that pair. If some preparation step ever sets currentSlot to targetSlot early, the new arm would skip a real install and report INSTALLED over an unwritten slot - a far worse defect than the one being fixed.

DO NOT LET THE NEW ARM WEAKEN IDENTITY CHECKING. settledInstall's preparedIdentity comparison is what stops one command adopting another's anchor. The new arm must carry the same check; dropping it in the name of 'the switch already landed' would let a different command claim a completed install.

THE PRE-SWITCH PREPARED CASE MUST STILL INSTALL. A PREPARED record whose currentSlot differs from targetSlot is the ordinary pre-switch state and must proceed normally. A condition written slightly too broadly would swallow it and silently skip real installs - which is why step 4 pins that case explicitly.

THE TEST MUST OBSERVE THE SEAM, NOT THE BYTES. The harm is that writeInactiveSlot and stampIncarnation RUN, not that the resulting bytes differ - after a successful completion the bytes may well look correct either way. Asserting on disk content could pass while the protocol was re-entered.

recovery-anchor-install.ts IS ALREADY OVER THE PER-FILE TARGET at 263 lines. Do not grow it; split if the helper does not fit.
